t.3.1: Having truly known the Self as indestructible and one, how can you, a steadfast knower of the Self, take delight in the acquisition of wealth?
t.3.2: Ah, from ignorance of the Self arises delight in the sphere of the illusion of sense-objects, just as, from ignorance of the mother-of-pearl, greed arises in the illusion that it is silver.
t.3.3: Having realized, "I am That in which this universe shimmers like waves upon the ocean," why do you run about like a wretched man?
t.3.4: Even after hearing that the Self is pure consciousness and supremely beautiful, one who remains utterly attached to sexual pleasure falls into impurity.
t.3.6: It is a wonder that one who has taken his stand in the supreme non-duality and is firmly set upon the goal of liberation should still be under the sway of desire, unsettled by the practice of amorous play.
t.3.5: It is astonishing that the sense of 'mine' still persists in the sage who knows the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self!
t.3.7: Though he has recognized the enemy of knowledge that has arisen, it is a wonder that one who is utterly feeble and has reached his final hour should still eagerly long for it.
t.3.8: How strange it is that one who is detached from this world and the next, who discerns the eternal from the transient, and who longs for liberation should yet be terrified of liberation itself!
t.3.9: But the wise one, whether being fed or being tormented, always seeing the Self as alone, is neither pleased nor angered.
t.3.10: The great-souled one sees his own body in action as if it were the body of another; how then could he be disturbed by praise or by blame?
t.3.11: Seeing this universe as mere illusion, with all curiosity gone, how can one of steady mind fear even when death is near?
t.3.12: The great soul whose mind is free from desire even in the absence of all hope, who is content with the knowledge of the Self, with whom can he be compared?
t.3.14: For one who has inwardly cast off all impurities, who is free from the pairs of opposites and without desire, enjoyment that comes of its own accord brings neither sorrow nor satisfaction.
t.3.13: Knowing by his very nature that this visible world is nothing at all, what could the one of steady intellect see as 'this is to be grasped' and 'this is to be abandoned'?
